name: Adam Cohen
title: John P. Reardon Jr. Professor of Chemistry & Chemical Biology and of Physics (Accepting Graduate Students)
research_summary: Research Areas Biophysics Chemical Biology Physical/Chemical Physics Theoretical
ai_review: Adam Cohen’s research program in Chemistry centers on applying biophysical and theoretical methods to investigate fundamental questions in chemical biology and physical/chemical physics. His lab primarily focuses on understanding protein dynamics and interactions, employing techniques like molecular dynamics simulations and advanced spectroscopic measurements – such as fluorescence spectroscopy – to characterize conformational changes and binding events within biological systems. Cohen’s work often involves developing novel computational models and algorithms to analyze complex data sets related to protein folding, aggregation, and the effects of environmental factors on biomolecular behavior.  Specifically, he investigates how these processes are influenced by chemical perturbations and utilizes a combination of experimental and theoretical approaches for detailed investigation. Ultimately, his research seeks to provide deeper insights into the physical principles governing biological function at the molecular level.

name: David R. Liu
title: Thomas Dudley Cabot Professor of the Natural Sciences Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator (Accepting Graduate Students)
research_summary: Research Areas Bioorganic Chemical Biology Organic Origins of Life
ai_review: David R. Liu’s research program in Chemistry centers on exploring the origins of life through a fascinating intersection of bioorganic chemistry and chemical biology, specifically investigating “Organic Origins of Life.” His lab utilizes sophisticated synthetic organic chemistry techniques to construct and test novel biochemical systems, with a particular focus on understanding how early Earth environments may have fostered the emergence of self-replicating molecules. Dr. Liu's work delves into the design and characterization of chemically synthesized analogs of ribozymes and other RNA components, seeking to recreate conditions relevant to prebiotic chemistry. Through these experimental investigations—often employing techniques like solution NMR spectroscopy and advanced chromatographic methods—the lab aims to identify key chemical pathways involved in the transition from non-life to life. Ultimately, Dr. Liu’s research seeks to illuminate fundamental questions regarding the initial steps of biological evolution.

name: Emily Balskus
title: Thomas Dudley Cabot Professor of Chemistry Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator (Accepting Graduate Students)
research_summary: Research Areas Bioorganic Chemical Biology Organic
ai_review: Emily Balskus’s research in the Chemistry department centers on the fascinating intersection of bioorganic chemical biology, specifically focusing on the intricate interactions between synthetic molecules and biological systems. Her lab investigates the structural and functional properties of microbial surface polysaccharides, employing techniques such as NMR spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, and cryo-electron microscopy to characterize these complex carbohydrate networks. Balskus’s work particularly emphasizes understanding how bacteria utilize these polysaccharides for biofilm formation and dispersal – processes with significant implications for human health and environmental science. Ultimately, her research aims to develop novel strategies for disrupting bacterial communities and mitigating the spread of infectious diseases through targeted manipulation of microbial surface carbohydrates.

name: Eric Heller
title: Abbott and James Lawrence Professor of Chemistry Professor of Physics (Accepting Graduate Students)
research_summary: Research Areas Materials Physical/Chemical Physics Theoretical
ai_review: Eric Heller’s research program in the Chemistry Department focuses on utilizing theoretical and computational methods to investigate fundamental physical and chemical phenomena, particularly within materials science. His work centers around developing and applying density functional theory (DFT) calculations to study complex molecular systems and condensed matter physics, with a significant emphasis on understanding charge transfer processes and excited state dynamics in semiconductors and other materials. Specifically, Professor Heller’s lab investigates the electronic structure of organic photovoltaic materials and explores phenomena like Förster resonance energy transfer, employing sophisticated simulations to predict material properties and behavior under various conditions. Through this research, he aims to contribute to advancements in areas such as solar energy conversion and optoelectronic devices.

name: Kang-Kuen Ni
title: Theodore William Richards Professor of Chemistry and Professor of Physics (Accepting Graduate Students)
ai_review: Kang-Kuen Ni’s research within the Chemistry department focuses on the intricate physical and chemical physics of materials, primarily investigating the behavior of molecules and their interactions in complex systems. Her lab utilizes advanced spectroscopic techniques, including femtosecond pump-probe spectroscopy and electron spin resonance (ESR), to probe dynamics at extremely short timescales – from picoseconds to nanoseconds – within biological and inorganic samples. Specifically, Dr. Ni’s work centers on understanding energy transfer processes in photosynthetic reaction centres and the role of paramagnetic impurities in influencing excited state dynamics.  Through this detailed experimental analysis, she aims to elucidate fundamental mechanisms governing light harvesting and energy dissipation within these systems, contributing significantly to our knowledge of both biological and advanced materials science.

ai_review: Suzanne Walker’s research group within the Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology at Harvard Medical School investigates fundamental microbial processes through an interdisciplinary approach combining microbiology, molecular genetics, and cutting-edge technologies. The Walker lab primarily focuses on understanding bacterial cell division, specifically exploring the mechanisms governing chromosome segregation and the role of key proteins like ParM in constructing Z-rings. Utilizing techniques such as fluorescence microscopy, genetic manipulation (including CRISPR-Cas9), and biochemical assays, the group aims to elucidate how bacteria maintain genomic stability during replication. Their work contributes significantly to broader questions regarding cell biology and has implications for understanding antibiotic resistance and developing novel strategies for controlling bacterial populations.  Notably, Professor Walker’s research leverages smartphone technology for data collection within their experiments.

name: Theodore Betley
title: Erving Professor of Chemistry Director of Graduate Studies (Accepting Graduate Students)
research_summary: Research Areas Analytical Catalysis Energy Related Inorganic Organometallics
ai_review: Theodore Betley’s research program in Chemistry focuses on utilizing analytical catalysis to address challenges within energy-related inorganic organometallics. His lab investigates novel catalytic systems, primarily employing transition metal complexes, to facilitate reactions relevant to sustainable chemistry and the development of clean fuel sources. Specifically, Professor Betley's work centers around designing and characterizing catalysts for CO₂ reduction and other transformations involving light absorption and subsequent chemical reactivity – often utilizing spectroscopic techniques like UV-Vis spectroscopy and X-ray adsorption spectroscopy to understand reaction mechanisms. Through this approach, he seeks to engineer materials with enhanced activity and selectivity for critical energy applications, representing a significant contribution to the field of organometallic catalysis.

ai_review: Tim Kaxiras’s research within the Chemistry and Applied Computational Science Institute at Harvard University centers on utilizing computational methods, particularly molecular dynamics simulations, to investigate complex biological processes. His work primarily focuses on understanding protein folding, aggregation, and interactions – areas crucial for elucidating disease mechanisms and designing novel therapeutics. Leveraging advanced computing resources, including smartphone-based calculations, Kaxiras’s lab employs techniques like all-atom simulations to model the dynamic behavior of biomolecules at an atomic level.  He actively engages with the Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology through his affiliation and currently accepts graduate students, fostering research within this interdisciplinary space. Ultimately, Kaxiras’s group aims to translate computational insights into a deeper understanding of fundamental chemical principles governing biological systems.

name: Xiaowei Zhuang
title: David B. Arnold, Jr. Professor of Science Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator (Accepting Graduate Students)
ai_review: Xiaowei Zhuang’s research program within the Chemistry Department investigates fundamental biological processes through the lens of biophysics and physical chemistry. Her lab primarily focuses on utilizing fluorescence microscopy, particularly super-resolution techniques like STORM and PALM, to visualize molecular dynamics and interactions within living cells. Specifically, Professor Zhuang's work centers around characterizing protein organization, focusing extensively on actin filaments and their role in cellular mechanics and signaling pathways. Employing advanced image analysis methods and biophysical assays, her research seeks to understand how these dynamic structures contribute to complex biological phenomena with implications for areas like cancer metastasis and neuronal function. Ultimately, Zhuang’s lab utilizes cutting-edge optical microscopy to dissect the physical principles governing life at a molecular scale.
